newsitem.title: UK: Lloyd's to publish underwriting codes of practice.
newsitem.headline: Lloyd's to publish underwriting codes of practice.

text.p: Lloyd's of London is expected shortly to publish proposed codes of practice for the insurance market's underwriting agents, industry sources said on Tuesday.

The consultation document on managing underwriting risk is another step towards the insurance market's goal of establishing a comprehensive system of internal controls designed to police effectively the activities of its professional members.
Lloyd's wants to be more in line with other financial markets, which already have their own well defined codes of practice. It is at present governed by parliamentary by-laws.

The latest guidelines are designed to show managing agents how to control underwriting risk and include recommendations that they set up teams comprising their own senior executives to review regularly the performance of underwriting syndicates.

"We would like to think the kinds of controls in there (the document) are those normally in place elsewhere. It's all about making the board aware of their responsibilities," said a source at the insurance market.
Lloyd's expects managing agents to comply with the guidelines unless they show they can manage underwriting risk as effectively by some other method.
The insurance market has asked its members for comments on the draft code by October 4.

The document comes as the insurance market waits for the British Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) to decide whether or not to approve its proposed recovery plan. Lloyd's said last week that it had enough support to declare its 3.2 billion stg settlement offer to individual investors (Names) unconditional, with 91 percent of them accepting it.
Under the terms of the recovery plan, the settlement offer is designed to offset the cost to Names of reinsuring into a new company called Equitas and to end litigation.
If the DTI approves the recovery plan, as chairman David Rowland hopes it will do this week, Lloyd's future is secure.

But then the market's management will increasingly focus its efforts on trying to create the right environment for a new breed of capital provider -- the corporate investor -- and at the same time establish a more suitable regulatory framework.
Some of this work is already underway and the underwriting codes of practice are part of these efforts. They follow rules introduced last month overhauling Lloyd's disciplinary regime.

Rowland has said regulation of the insurance market in the future may be divided -- with Lloyd's itself supervising professional members, and investor protection falling to an outside body like the Securities and Investments Board.
